issues.legal_issue: A contractual arbitration clause does not displace the civil court’s jurisdiction over a landlord-tenant dispute seeking eviction and related reliefs.
material_facts: The landlord filed a civil suit seeking the tenant’s eviction, unpaid rent and a permanent injunction concerning leased commercial premises.
The lease had expired, no renewed lease was executed, and the tenancy continued monthly.
The lease contained an arbitration clause covering disputes arising from it.
The tenant sought referral to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit was maintainable, and the tenant’s application for referral to arbitration was correctly dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios, which held that a landlord-tenant possession dispute was for the designated court and not an arbitrator, and Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd., which identifies certain eviction and tenancy disputes as non-arbitrable, the Court held that an arbitration clause did not require this eviction dispute to be referred to arbitration. Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 did not require referral in these circumstances.

rule.if: defendant_sought_arbitration_referral and landlord_tenant_relationship and eviction_or_possession_dispute and lease_contains_arbitration_clause

predicates.defendant_sought_arbitration_referral: The defendant asked for the dispute in a pending civil suit to be referred to arbitration.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship: The parties’ dispute arose from their relationship as landlord and tenant.
predicates.eviction_or_possession_dispute: The civil suit sought the tenant’s eviction or recovery of possession of leased premises.
predicates.lease_contains_arbitration_clause: The lease between the parties contained a clause providing for arbitration of disputes.

issues.definition: When a defendant seeks arbitration in a civil suit arising from a landlord-tenant relationship, and the suit concerns eviction or possession under a lease containing an arbitration clause, the civil court may decide the eviction dispute.

issues.legal_issue: Exclusion of premises from rent-control legislation does not make a landlord-tenant eviction or rent dispute arbitrable merely because the lease contains an arbitration clause.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the Delhi Rent Act did not apply to the premises because they fell within an exclusion in that Act.
The suit sought eviction and ancillary reliefs concerning a tenancy for which no renewed lease had been executed after the original term expired.
The lease contained an arbitration clause.

The Court stated that, where the rent-control statute does not apply to premises, the parties’ rights are governed by the Transfer of Property Act and the civil suit is triable by a civil court, not an arbitrator.
issues.conclusion: The rent-control exclusion did not make the arbitration law applicable so as to confer jurisdiction on an arbitrator; the dispute was triable by the civil court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 3 of the Delhi Rent Act, 1955, and held that its non-application to particular premises does not, by itself, confer jurisdiction on an arbitrator. For premises outside the Act’s application, rights are governed by the Transfer of Property Act and a civil suit is triable by the civil court. The Court relied on Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios and Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd. in holding that the dispute was not to be referred to arbitration.

predicates.rent_control_exclusion: The premises fall outside the coverage of the rent-control regime governing the tenancy.
predicates.landlord_tenant_rent_or_eviction_dispute: The dispute concerns rent, eviction, or possession between a landlord and a tenant.
predicates.civil_suit_filed: A party brought the landlord-tenant dispute in a civil court.

issues.definition: When premises fall outside rent-control coverage and a civil suit concerns rent, eviction, or possession between landlord and tenant, the dispute is decided by the civil court rather than an arbitrator.
